title: Your own functions and apply
setup:
import pandas as pd
df = pd.read_csv("games.csv")
explanation: Welcome to Level 5: pro skills! A function is a reusable recipe you name yourself. Start with def, then the name and an input in brackets, then a colon. The indented lines below are the recipe, and return sends back the answer. Indenting (4 spaces) is how Python knows which lines belong to the function. To run your function on every value in a column, use apply(): df["price"].apply(my_function). For tiny one-line recipes, a lambda is a nameless shortcut: df["price"].apply(lambda p: p * 2).

lines.explain: Start a function called to_cents that takes one input, price.
The recipe: multiply by 100, round, and send the answer back. Note the 4-space indent.

tasks.prompt: Predict first: what will this print?
hints: double(21) runs the recipe with x set to 21.

tasks.prompt: Fill in the blank so add_tax adds 8% tax (multiply by 1.08).
hints: Adding 8% is the same as multiplying by 1.08.

tasks.prompt: Use the to_cents function from the example on the price column (with apply). Store it as a cents column, then show title and cents.
hints: Define the function first, then df["cents"] = df["price"].apply(to_cents). Note: no brackets after to_cents inside apply.
def to_cents(price): / return round(price * 100), then df["cents"] = df["price"].apply(to_cents), then df[["title", "cents"]]

tasks.prompt: apply works with built-in functions too. Add a title_length column using apply(len), then show the title and title_length of the game with the longest title.
hints: len counts the characters in text. Then nlargest(1, ...) finds the biggest.

solution_lines.explain: Count the characters in every title.
Animal Crossing: New Horizons, with 29 characters.

tasks.prompt: Use a lambda to show every price with a 20% discount (price × 0.8), rounded to 2 decimals.
hints: lambda p: ... is a one-line function where p is each price.

solution_lines.explain: A nameless recipe: take p, return 80% of it, rounded.

recap: You just learned to write your own functions with def and return, run them on whole columns with apply(), and use lambda for quick one-liners.
